Describe the inauguration ceremony of Nelson Mandela on 10 May 1994.
questions.answer: On 10 May 1994 at the sandstone amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria, Mandela was inaugurated as the FIRST BLACK PRESIDENT of South Africa. He took the oath of office, joined on stage by his daughter ZENANI and his deputies F.W. de KLERK and Thabo MBEKI. The new South African flag was raised; the African anthem 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika' and the old anthem were sung side by side; the South African Air Force performed a fly-past in the new colours. Dignitaries from all over the world were present. The day formally ended three centuries of white rule and the system of apartheid.

questions.question: What was apartheid? Describe its main features.
questions.answer: APARTHEID is an Afrikaans word meaning 'separateness'. It was the official policy of the South African government from 1948, after the white-supremacist National Party won the election. Under apartheid, laws strictly segregated the country by race: BLACK AFRICANS were forced to carry passes, were removed to far-off 'homelands', and were denied the vote, decent education, good jobs, good housing and equal access to public spaces. Schools, hospitals, parks and beaches were segregated. The system formally ended in 1991 when apartheid laws were repealed; Mandela was inaugurated President in 1994.

questions.question: What does Mandela mean by 'twin obligations'? Why could a black man not fulfil them under apartheid?
questions.answer: Mandela writes that every man has two obligations in life: an OBLIGATION TO HIS FAMILY (his parents, wife and children) and an OBLIGATION TO HIS PEOPLE (his community and country). In a free society, each person can fulfil both naturally. But under APARTHEID, a black man could fulfil neither — to do his duty to his people forced him into conflict with the state, often at the cost of family. Children grew up without fathers (in prison or in exile); fathers carrying their daughters to the doctor were stopped at the colour line. The system therefore SHATTERED ordinary lives — making both family and public duty impossible.

questions.question: What does Mandela teach us about courage and hate?
questions.answer: Mandela writes that COURAGE is not the absence of fear, but the TRIUMPH OVER IT. The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid — fear is natural; the brave man is he who CONQUERS that fear. About HATE, Mandela writes that no one is born hating another person because of his skin colour or background; people LEARN to hate. And if they can be taught to hate, they can also be TAUGHT TO LOVE — for love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite. These two ideas became guiding lights for the Truth and Reconciliation Commission that healed South Africa after apartheid.

questions.question: How did Mandela's understanding of FREEDOM evolve from boyhood to adulthood?
questions.answer: AS A YOUNG BOY in his Transkei village, Mandela thought of freedom as the right to RUN, SWIM, PLOUGH, RIDE and walk the village — the simple physical freedom of a child. AS A YOUNG MAN in Johannesburg, he learned that freedom is more than physical movement — it is the right to LIVE A LIFE OF DIGNITY: to MARRY, RAISE A FAMILY, FOLLOW A PROFESSION. AS AN ADULT, he came to understand that freedom is INDIVISIBLE: no one is truly free if all are not free; the OPPRESSOR is as unfree as the oppressed, since both are imprisoned by hatred and prejudice. So freedom moved from PHYSICAL → CIVIL → MORAL — from the boy's freedom to the citizen's freedom to the whole nation's and humanity's freedom.

questions.question: What does Mandela say about apartheid as a 'human disaster'?
questions.answer: Mandela calls apartheid 'an extraordinary human disaster' that created 'a deep and lasting wound' on his country and his people. The wound was political (the denial of the vote, of citizenship, of dignity); economic (the denial of decent jobs, education, land); social (forced separation, broken families); and psychological (the daily humiliation of being treated as inferior). Mandela acknowledged the wound at the inauguration so that healing could begin. He also said that the same struggle had given South Africa 'men of such extraordinary courage, wisdom and generosity' — a balance of grief and gratitude.

questions.question: Briefly trace Nelson Mandela's life from boyhood to presidency.
questions.answer: Born 1918 in the Transkei region. As a young man he became a LAWYER and joined the AFRICAN NATIONAL CONGRESS (ANC) to fight apartheid. He led nonviolent and later armed resistance and was arrested. On 12 JUNE 1964 he was sentenced to LIFE IMPRISONMENT and held mostly on ROBBEN ISLAND for 27 YEARS, doing hard labour and writing his autobiography in secret. International pressure and continued resistance forced the white government to negotiate. He was RELEASED IN 1990. APARTHEID LAWS WERE REPEALED IN 1991. The first multi-racial democratic election was held on 27 APRIL 1994; the ANC won; on 10 MAY 1994 Mandela was inaugurated as the FIRST BLACK PRESIDENT of South Africa. He served one term (1994–99) and died in 2013.

questions.question: Describe the structure of 'A Tiger in the Zoo'.
questions.answer: The poem has FIVE STANZAS of FOUR LINES each — twenty lines in total. The structure is ALTERNATION: stanzas 1, 3 and 5 show the tiger IN HIS CAGE — pacing, ignoring visitors, staring at the stars at night. Stanzas 2 and 4 show a contrasting image of the tiger as he WOULD BE in the wild — sliding through long grass, lurking near a water-hole to ambush deer, snarling near a village. The rhyme scheme is ABCB — the second and fourth lines of each stanza rhyme. The strong, simple verbs (pads, slides, lurks, snarls, terrorises, stares) do most of the work, making the poem vivid without being long.

questions.question: What contrast does Norris draw between the caged tiger and the wild tiger?
questions.answer: CAGED TIGER — paces slowly back and forth on PADS OF VELVET behind the BARS OF HIS CAGE. He IGNORES visitors. At night, he hears the patrol car and the silence and stares at the brilliant stars longing for a freedom he cannot have. WILD TIGER — slides through LONG GRASS in his element; LURKS near a WATER-HOLE to ambush deer; or terrorises a VILLAGE by snarling near its huts. The contrast is between SLOW PACING and SWIFT MOVEMENT, BARS and OPEN GRASS, PASSIVE GAZE and ACTIVE HUNT, and ULTIMATELY between CAPTIVITY and FREEDOM. Each stanza enacts the contrast through verb, image and rhythm.

questions.question: What is the indirect message of 'A Tiger in the Zoo' about zoos and freedom?
questions.answer: Norris does not lecture the reader; he just SHOWS — caged tiger, wild tiger, caged tiger, wild tiger, caged tiger at night staring at the stars. The contrast carries the argument: the cage DIMINISHES the tiger. He still has dignity (he ignores visitors, paces with care, watches the stars), but his nature — his hunting power, his sliding through grass, his fear-inducing presence — is GONE. Zoos rob wild creatures of what makes them themselves. The poem is therefore an indirect critique of zoos and a meditation on what FREEDOM means for any living being. By making us SEE rather than TELLING us, the poem leaves the conclusion to the reader — and so the conclusion sticks.

questions.question: How are Mandela's piece and 'A Tiger in the Zoo' connected?
questions.answer: Both pieces are about FREEDOM, viewed from OPPOSITE poles. Mandela writes from the SIDE OF NEW FREEDOM — the day a long imprisonment ends, the tribute to comrades, the long walk that brought him there, the long walk still ahead. The voice is calm, public, factual. Norris writes from the SIDE OF ONGOING CAPTIVITY — through the imagined eye of a tiger pacing in a cage, longing for jungle. The voice is quiet, intimate, and shows rather than argues. Together the pieces tell us: WINNING freedom for an entire people takes generations of work; LOSING it — even for a single creature — diminishes the whole self. Mandela's deep insight that 'the oppressor is as unfree as the oppressed' echoes in the tiger poem: the cage diminishes the JAILER as well as the prisoner.

questions.question: What does Mandela mean by saying that 'the oppressor is as unfree as the oppressed'? Discuss with examples from the chapter.
questions.answer: Mandela's insight is that FREEDOM is INDIVISIBLE: where one group denies freedom to another, BOTH ARE TRAPPED. The OPPRESSED are the obvious prisoners — they lose vote, dignity, education, freedom of movement, often family and life. But the OPPRESSOR is also a prisoner — of HATRED (which deforms his soul), of PREJUDICE (which prevents him from seeing the human in the other), and of FEAR (the constant anxiety of maintaining a system that requires force, lies and the surveillance of others). EXAMPLES FROM THE CHAPTER — (i) The white police, judges, prison guards and politicians of apartheid South Africa lived their entire lives within a system whose maintenance required them to TREAT FELLOW HUMANS AS LESS THAN HUMAN — a daily violence to their own conscience. (ii) The white minority lived in fear of the black majority — their cities were policed, their daily life shadowed by the question: what if the system breaks? (iii) Mandela's own RECONCILIATION with former enemies (de Klerk became his deputy) showed that releasing the oppressed also LIBERATES the oppressor from the moral burden of injustice. WIDER MEANING — Mandela's point applies beyond apartheid: in any society where one group dominates another by force or law, BOTH lose. The free society is the one where everyone is free. This is also why the chapter's tiger poem rings so deeply: the cage diminishes the keeper as well as the kept.

questions.question: Discuss Mandela's ideas of COURAGE and LOVE as expressed in the excerpt. How are they connected to his political philosophy?
questions.answer: Mandela writes two of his most quoted lines in this excerpt: 'COURAGE was not the absence of fear, but the TRIUMPH OVER IT', and on hate, 'No one is born hating another person... if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to LOVE, for love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite'. These ideas are CONNECTED to his political philosophy in three ways. (i) BOTH ARE LEARNED. Courage is not innate; it is built by people CHOOSING to act in the face of fear. Love and hate are not innate either; they are learned from family, society, education. (ii) BOTH POWER NON-VIOLENT STRUGGLE. Mandela's ANC and the wider anti-apartheid movement included people who CHOSE to act despite fear of arrest, imprisonment, torture and death. They also CHOSE to love (or at least respect) their oppressors enough not to seek vengeance — a discipline that allowed reconciliation later. (iii) BOTH UNDERPIN POST-APARTHEID HEALING. The TRUTH AND RECONCILIATION COMMISSION (chaired by Bishop Tutu after 1995) was built on the idea that public TELLING of the truth — combined with a willingness to FORGIVE — could heal the country. That commission would have been impossible if Mandela had not REPEATEDLY MODELLED courage (forgiving his jailers, embracing de Klerk) and love (talking of a 'rainbow nation', integrating institutions). Mandela's ideas of courage and love are therefore not just personal beliefs — they were the SCAFFOLDING for South Africa's transition from a divided, violent past to a shared, democratic future. They remain a model for any society trying to overcome historical wrongs.

questions.question: Critically discuss 'A Tiger in the Zoo' as a study of freedom and captivity. Do you find the indirect approach effective?
questions.answer: Norris's poem is a small masterpiece of indirect argument. Five stanzas of four lines each. No moralising. No statement that 'zoos are bad' or 'tigers should be free'. Just images. STANZA 1 — caged tiger pacing on PADS OF VELVET. STANZA 2 — wild tiger sliding through LONG GRASS, lurking near a WATER-HOLE. STANZA 3 — caged tiger ignoring visitors. STANZA 4 — wild tiger TERRORISING a village. STANZA 5 — caged tiger at night, the city silent, staring at the BRILLIANT STARS. THE STUDY OF FREEDOM AND CAPTIVITY — through the contrast, the poem shows what is LOST when a wild creature is caged: its environment (grass, water, forest), its hunting power, its capacity to SHAPE the lives of those around it (terrorising a village), its right to be itself. What remains: the SLOW PACE, the IGNORE, the FAR-OFF GAZE. The tiger has not lost his dignity — he ignores the gawking crowd, paces with care, watches the stars. But he has lost almost everything else. EFFECTIVENESS OF THE INDIRECT APPROACH — In my view, the indirect approach is HIGHLY EFFECTIVE. (i) It RESPECTS the reader. Norris does not preach; he TRUSTS the reader to draw the lesson. (ii) It IS HARDER TO ARGUE WITH. A direct lecture about zoos invites disagreement; the IMAGE of the tiger staring at the stars is harder to dismiss. (iii) It STAYS in the memory. Years after reading, one remembers the velvet pads and the brilliant stars more than any thesis. (iv) It LINKS to wider freedom. Without ever mentioning humans, the poem connects to every prisoner — including Nelson Mandela on Robben Island, and through him, to every person constrained by unjust systems. CONCLUSION — Norris's poem is a quiet companion to Mandela's grand prose. Together they remind us that freedom matters at every scale — from the soul of a single tiger to the soul of a nation.

questions.question: What unifies Mandela's prose and Norris's poem as Chapter 2 of First Flight? Discuss the chapter as a meditation on freedom.
questions.answer: At first glance the two pieces are very different — a great political autobiography about the inauguration of a country's first black president, and a small twenty-line poem about a tiger in a zoo. But they are paired because both meditate on FREEDOM — from OPPOSITE poles. MANDELA from the FREEDOM SIDE — the day a long imprisonment ends; the public ceremony, the new flag, the African anthem, the tribute to comrades, the embracing of former enemies, the long walk that brought him to that day, the long walk still ahead. The voice is CALM, PUBLIC, FACTUAL. The piece is large in scale: a whole nation, three centuries of injustice, the redemption of millions. NORRIS from the CAPTIVITY SIDE — the imagined eye of a tiger pacing in a zoo, alternating with images of his lost wild life. The voice is QUIET, INTIMATE, IMAGE-BASED. The piece is small in scale: a single creature, a single cage, a single night gaze at the stars. THE CONNECTION — both pieces ask, WHAT IS FREEDOM? Mandela answers BIG: freedom is the right of an entire people to dignity, work, family, vote, future. Norris answers SMALL: freedom is the right of a wild creature to its true environment and its own nature. Both answers are TRUE. Mandela's deep insight that 'the oppressor is as unfree as the oppressed' connects the two pieces: just as apartheid imprisoned both blacks and whites, the tiger's cage diminishes both keeper and kept. THE DEEPER MESSAGE — across both pieces, freedom emerges as INDIVISIBLE and HARD-WON. Winning it for an entire people takes the work of generations and a long walk. Losing it — even for a single creature — is to lose oneself, even if one paces with the dignity of a tiger. The chapter is therefore a study of freedom at every scale — political, personal, animal. It teaches the reader to value freedom, to honour those who fight for it, and to recognise its absence wherever it occurs.
